candidate.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance client-needs subcategory (6–12% of items); this item tests client education for recognition and reduction of modifiable exposures that can worsen a chronic health condition.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Health-promotion teaching for recognition and reduction of asthma triggers
candidate.educational_objective: Teach clients with asthma to identify their own symptom triggers, which may include allergens, respiratory infections, exercise, smoke or other irritants, and poor air quality, and incorporate trigger reduction into an individualized asthma-management plan.

options.A: Allergens, viral respiratory infections, physical activity, and poor air quality or other inhaled irritants
options.B: Only one universal trigger that is the same for every person with asthma
options.C: Triggers that are relevant only during childhood and no longer affect adults with asthma
options.D: Only prescribed asthma medications, because environmental and infectious exposures do not worsen asthma

candidate.rationale: A is correct. Current NHLBI guidance identifies common asthma triggers including indoor and outdoor allergens, infections such as colds and influenza, physical activity, and poor air quality or cold air. Current CDC guidance likewise emphasizes that triggers differ among people with asthma and includes smoke, allergens, infections, chemicals or fragrances, weather, and exercise among recognized triggers. B is incorrect because triggers are individualized. C is incorrect because asthma triggers affect adults as well as children. D contradicts current federal guidance on environmental, infectious, and activity-related triggers.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Current federal guidance directly supports allergens, respiratory infections, physical activity, poor air quality, smoke, and other irritants as recognized asthma triggers and explicitly supports individualized trigger identification rather than a universal trigger list for every client.
candidate.source_document_title: Asthma — Causes and Triggers; Managing Asthma; Controlling Asthma
candidate.source_locator: NHLBI 'Asthma — Causes and Triggers' → 'Asthma triggers': common triggers include indoor/outdoor allergens, physical activity, infections such as colds/flu/COVID-19, and poor air quality or very cold air. NHLBI 'Managing Asthma' → 'Know your asthma triggers': avoid identified allergens, infection exposures, air pollution, tobacco smoke, and other personal triggers. CDC 'Controlling Asthma' → Key Points: triggers can differ from one person with asthma to another; common triggers include secondhand smoke, dust mites, air pollution, mold, respiratory infections, pollen/allergies, chemicals/fragrances, weather, and physical exercise.
candidate.source_organization: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI/NIH), corroborated by Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidate.source_version_date: NHLBI asthma pages last updated 2024-04-17 and current at access 2026-08-18; CDC Controlling Asthma page dated 2024-01-22 and current at access 2026-08-18; current 2026 CDC/NIOSH asthma resources also continue to identify allergens, irritants, and physical exertion as triggers
candidate.stem: A nurse helps a client with asthma identify personal triggers that can worsen symptoms. Which group contains recognized asthma triggers?
